title: Lower step rate is associated with a higher risk of bone stress injury: a prospective study of collegiate cross country runners
authors: Kliethermes SA, Stiffler-Joachim MR, Wille CM, Sanfilippo JL, Zavala P, Heiderscheit BC
population: 54 NCAA Division I cross country runners over three consecutive seasons, preseason treadmill biomechanics and DXA BMD, medically diagnosed BSI followed 12 months
findings: Univariably, step rate, centre of mass vertical excursion, peak vertical GRF and vertical GRF impulse were associated with BSI incidence.
After adjusting for BSI history and sex, each 1 step/min higher step rate was associated with 5% lower BSI risk (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.91-0.98).
BMD z-score was not a statistically significant predictor in the final model (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.85-1.03).
No other biomechanical variables were independently associated with BSI risk.
limitations: 54 collegiate runners; single preseason measurement; observational so causality of cadence is untested; collegiate competitive athletes, not general recreational runners.
implications: Cadence from watch data can be a displayed risk context for bone stress only; do not prescribe cadence changes from this evidence.
No change to load-progression rules is justified.

verification.notes: Crossref: BJSM 55:851-856 (online May 2021), 6 authors (the author list is complete). Abstract matched. Removed the speculative 'low cadence plus rapid increases' combined rule.
